1Password (formerly AgileBits) · Canada · Official site ↗ · Affiliate program (public, reported)

The premium consumer password manager, expanded into an enterprise identity platform (Unified Access) in 2026. Known for app polish, the two-secret security model (master password + Secret Key), Watchtower breach monitoring, and family-friendly sharing.

Pricing (verified framing)

Individual $3.99/mo (≈$47.88/yr, $2.99 first-year promo); Families $5.99/mo for up to 5 members ($4.49 first-year promo); 14-day trial; no free tier. Verified 2026-09-06 on official pages. Business is quote-led.

Strengths

  • Best-in-class app polish
  • Secret Key two-secret architecture
  • Watchtower security dashboard
  • Smooth family sharing and recovery
  • Developer tooling (SSH agent, CLI)

Weaknesses

  • No free tier
  • ≈2× Bitwarden Premium at regular pricing
  • Closed source; no self-hosting
  • First-year promos revert

item.title: 1Password Review (2026): Premium Polish, Premium Price — Who Should Pay It
item.dc:creator: readmehub
item.content:encoded:
Executive verdict

1Password is the most polished password manager we researched: the apps, organization, Watchtower breach monitoring and family sharing set the category's experience benchmark. That polish is the product — and the price. At $3.99/mo regular with no free tier, it earns its cost for households and professionals who value a frictionless experience; budget-first users should start with Bitwarden.

Best for
  • Families who want sharing to 'just work'Unlimited shared vaults, simple admin controls, and per-member access — the most refined family UX in the category
  • Professionals who live in their vaultItem organization, Watchtower security alerts, and Travel Mode are best-in-class conveniences
  • New customers willing to try before buyingA 14-day full-feature trial — no crippled free tier to evaluate
Not ideal for
  • Budget-first usersThere is no free plan. Bitwarden's free tier covers unlimited passwords and devices for $0
  • Open-source purists1Password's clients are closed source; trust rests on vendor-documented third-party audits rather than public code
  • Self-hostersNo self-hosting option exists; your vault lives in 1Password's cloud

Key takeaways

  • Individual: $3.99/mo billed annually (≈$47.88/yr). New customers get a verified first-year promotion at $2.99/mo; year two reverts to $3.99.
  • Families: $5.99/mo (≈$71.88/yr) covering up to 5 invited members — about $1.00/person/mo at full occupancy. First-year promo: $4.49/mo.
  • No free tier; 14-day free trial on personal plans.
  • Security model: AES-256 encryption plus 1Password's unique Secret Key — a second, account-specific secret beyond your master password.
  • Closed source, with third-party security audits published by the vendor; no self-hosting.
  • 1Password's business positioning has shifted upmarket (its main pricing page now leads with the Unified Access platform); consumer plans live on the personal pricing page.

Pricing & plans — verified

Verified on 1Password's official pricing pages on 2026-09-06. Prices in USD, annual billing. Promotional first-year rates are for new customers only, per the vendor.

Business plans (Teams Starter, Business) are quoted via 1Password's business pages; figures reported by third parties in 2026 ranged around $7.99–8.99/user/mo. We have not verified current business pricing on the official page — check with 1Password before relying on a number.

Feature-by-feature analysis

Core vault & autofill

The most refined autofill and item-organization experience among the managers we researched — tagged collections, multiple vaults, and consistent apps across platforms (vendor-documented; corroborated by independent 2026 reviews).

Watchtower

Proactive security dashboard: breached-password alerts, weak/reused password flags, missing 2FA, and expiring items. A genuine differentiator in day-to-day use.

Secret Key architecture

Your vault is encrypted with AES-256 using a key derived from your master password AND a 128-bit Secret Key generated at signup. The practical upside: a leaked master password alone is not sufficient to decrypt your vault. The practical cost: lose the Secret Key (and Emergency Kit) and recovery is impossible.

Family sharing

Unlimited shared vaults with granular permissions and simple admin controls. Recovery of a family member's account is straightforward — a real-world feature most competitors handle worse.

Travel Mode

Removes vaults from devices when you travel, restoring them later. Niche, but unmatched if border searches matter to your threat model.

Passkeys & 2FA

Passkey storage/use and Watchtower-driven 2FA guidance are supported (vendor-documented). No integrated TOTP authenticator equivalent to Bitwarden Premium's — 1Password expects your 2FA codes elsewhere.

Developer tooling

SSH agent, CLI, and Secrets Automation are included — a genuine reason developers tolerate the premium (documented on 1Password's developer pages).

Ease of use

Based on documented evidence — 1Password's own UX documentation plus consistent independent assessments in 2026 — onboarding is the smoothest in the category: a guided setup, an Emergency Kit PDF pattern that makes Secret Key handling almost foolproof, and autofill that rarely needs intervention. We label this as evidence-based rather than tested-by-us.

Security

AES-256, zero-knowledge design, and the two-secret model (master password + Secret Key). Not open source; the vendor publishes third-party audit reports of its server and client software. Jurisdiction: Canada. 1Password has no known public breach of vault data. For the open-source alternative, see Bitwarden.

Pros & cons

Pros
  • Best-in-class app polish, organization, and family UX
  • Secret Key adds a second independent secret beyond the master password
  • Watchtower is the most actionable security dashboard we researched
  • 14-day full trial — evaluate everything before paying
  • First-year promotion ($2.99 Individual) verified for new customers
Cons
  • No free tier — the only launch-set manager without one
  • Regular price is roughly 2× Bitwarden Premium ($47.88 vs $19.80 per year)
  • Closed source; no self-hosting option
  • First-year promo reverts to $3.99/mo — budget for year two
  • Family plan caps at 5 invited members (Bitwarden Families covers 6 accounts)

Alternatives to consider first

  • NordPass — Choose if you want the cheapest polished paid tier and accept multi-year terms
  • Families
  • Current verified offers

FAQ

Is 1Password worth the price in 2026?
If you value a frictionless experience across devices and share a vault with family, yes — the polish is real and the family plan is about $1.00/person/mo at capacity. If price is your primary constraint, Bitwarden delivers the same security fundamentals for $19.80/yr — or $0. That trade-off is the entire 1Password-vs-Bitwarden decision.
How much does 1Password cost after the first year?
The verified regular prices are $3.99/mo for Individual and $5.99/mo for Families (annual billing). The $2.99/$4.49 figures are first-year promotions for new customers only, per 1Password's pricing page.
Does 1Password have a free plan?
No. 1Password offers a 14-day free trial instead. If you need a permanent free tier, Bitwarden and Proton Pass both offer genuinely usable free plans.
What happens if I lose my 1Password Secret Key?
Your Emergency Kit — generated at signup — is the recovery path for the Secret Key. Families admins can help members recover accounts. If both the Secret Key and Emergency Kit are lost, 1Password cannot decrypt your vault; that is the design, not a flaw.
The bottom line

Pay for polish when polish is what you need; don't pay for it when price is the constraint.

item.title: Bitwarden Review (2026): The Value and Transparency Benchmark
item.dc:creator: readmehub
item.content:encoded:
Executive verdict

Bitwarden is the benchmark for value and transparency: an unlimited free tier (every password, every device), open-source code you can audit, self-hosting if you want it, and Premium at $19.80/yr for the features most people eventually want. The trade-off is experience: its apps are less refined than 1Password's, and its web-vault-centric workflow can feel utilitarian.

  • Anyone who wants a genuinely free password managerThe free tier has no password or device limits — unique among mainstream managers

Executive verdict

NordPass is the cheapest polished paid tier in our research set — fast, friendly apps, breach scanner, password health — but the price is a function of commitment: multi-year terms, with 1-year and monthly billing costing noticeably more, and the free plan limited to one device. Choose it if you're comfortable with Nord Security's closed-source ecosystem and a longer commitment; choose Bitwarden if the term or the closed source bothers you.

Best for
  • Deal-driven buyers locking in multi-year termsLowest per-month cost for a polished, modern app among our verified set (longest terms)
  • Non-technical householdsSimple onboarding, clean UX, and a low-decision family plan (6 users)
  • Existing Nord ecosystem usersBundle pricing with NordVPN makes the combined value stronger than either alone
Not ideal for
  • Free-tier seekersThe free plan works on one device at a time — a real constraint for phone+laptop humans
  • Open-source and self-host advocatesClosed source, no self-hosting; trust rests on Nord Security's reputation and audits
  • Month-to-month buyersShort billing terms erase the price advantage that defines the product

Key takeaways

  • Free tier: unlimited passwords, but one active device at a time (corroborated by multiple 2026 sources).
  • Paid pricing is term-based: roughly $1.3–2/mo across 1–2 year terms in 2026 coverage — exact figures move with promotions and region, so we publish the range and link the official checkout rather than a number we can't guarantee.
  • Family plan covers 6 users at a per-month rate well below 1Password Families (term-dependent).
  • Encryption is XChaCha20 (rather than the category's usual AES-256) — a modern, respected choice, per NordPass documentation and multiple sources.
  • Includes data-breach scanner, password health, and emergency access on paid tiers (vendor-documented).
  • Closed source, owned by Nord Security (also NordVPN) — bundle context is part of the value story.

Pricing & plans — verified

NordPass prices by billing term and runs frequent regional promotions. We verified the plan structure on the official site on 2026-09-06; because per-month figures move with term and promotion, we state the verified range and route you to the live checkout for the exact number. We would rather show you a range than a fake certainty.

Why not exact numbers? Our policy: publish only prices verified at the official checkout at verification time. NordPass's dynamic promotions made a single stable figure unverifiable on 2026-09-06; the range above is corroborated by multiple 2026 sources and labeled as such.

Feature-by-feature analysis

Autofill & speed

Consistently described across independent 2026 coverage as among the fastest, least fussy autofill experiences — the 'easy on-ramp' pick. Evidence-based, not lab-tested by us.

Data Breach Scanner

Flags your emails and passwords against breach data on paid tiers. Comparable function to 1Password Watchtower's breach alerts, without the wider dashboard.

Password Health

Weak/reused password reporting on paid tiers — table stakes done cleanly.

Email masking

Email alias generation on paid tiers (vendor-documented) — handy, though Proton Pass includes 10 aliases even free.

Ecosystem & bundling

Nord Security sells NordPass alongside NordVPN and NordLocker; combined bundles improve total value if you want the suite. Single-product buyers should compare the effective price against Bitwarden Premium first.

Ease of use

Evidence-based: NordPass's onboarding is the gentlest in our set — import, browser extension, done. The app design (by the team behind NordVPN) prioritizes simplicity over depth, which is exactly right for non-technical households and exactly limiting for power users.

Security

XChaCha20 encryption, zero-knowledge design, no known vault breaches (as of our 2026-09-06 review). Closed source; Nord Security publishes audit information for its products (vendor-documented). Jurisdiction: Lithuania (EU). If open-source verification is your baseline, Bitwarden or Proton Pass fit better.

  • Cheapest polished paid tier in our research set (on long terms)
  • Fast, simple apps — the least intimidating onboarding
  • Family plan for 6 users undercuts 1Password Families substantially
  • Breach scanner and password health included on paid tiers
Cons

  • Closed source; no self-hosting
  • Best prices require 2-year commitments; monthly billing is comparatively expensive
  • Promotional pricing moves — you must verify the live checkout price

We publish the verified range rather than a specific number because NordPass's promotions change frequently — the official checkout shows your exact regional price.
    Is the NordPass free plan usable?
    Only for single-device users: free NordPass works on one device at a time, with unlimited password storage. If you bounce between a phone and a laptop, that constraint bites immediately — Bitwarden's unlimited free tier is the better free starting point.
    Is XChaCha20 encryption safe compared to AES-256?
    Yes — XChaCha20 is a modern, well-regarded stream cipher; the safety difference versus AES-256 is negligible for this use case. What matters more is the zero-knowledge architecture, which NordPass shares with the rest of our set.
    Is NordPass part of NordVPN?
    Both belong to Nord Security (same parent company). They are separate products with separate subscriptions, but bundling discounts exist — a genuine value factor if you want both.

    Great value if you commit; the wrong pick if you won't.

item.content:encoded:
Executive verdict

Proton Pass pairs the strongest privacy pedigree in our set — Swiss jurisdiction, open-source code, the team behind Proton Mail — with a genuinely usable free tier: unlimited logins, unlimited devices, even 10 email aliases. The honest caveat is maturity: the product is the youngest here, its app polish trails 1Password, and its most compelling extras (unlimited aliases, integrated 2FA) sit in paid tiers whose prices we couldn't pin to a verifiable figure on launch day — check the official pricing page for the live number.

Best for
  • Privacy-first usersSwiss jurisdiction, open source, and a company whose core business is encrypted communications
  • Anyone wanting a capable free tier plus aliasesUnlimited logins/devices and 10 hide-my-email aliases free (verified on the official pricing page)
  • Existing Proton ecosystem usersPass is included in Proton Unlimited alongside Mail, VPN, Calendar, and Drive
Not ideal for
  • Users who want the most mature, polished apps today1Password remains the experience benchmark; Pass's apps are newer and less refined
  • Buyers who need published stable pricing to planPaid-tier prices render dynamically and promotions move; verify at checkout before budgeting

Key takeaways

  • Free tier verified (official pricing page, 2026-09-06): unlimited logins, notes, credit cards; unlimited devices; password generator; 10 hide-my-email aliases; passkey support; weak/reused password alerts.
  • Pass Plus adds (verified feature list): unlimited aliases, integrated 2FA authenticator, secure vault/item sharing, dark-web monitoring, file attachments, emergency access, custom-domain aliases, CLI.
  • Pass Family covers 6 users; Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Mail/VPN/Calendar/Drive.
  • 30-day money-back guarantee on paid plans (verified) — effectively a risk-free trial.
  • Open source; Swiss jurisdiction (strong privacy law); vendor-reported 100M+ Proton user base.
  • We do not publish Pass Plus/Family dollar figures: the official page renders prices dynamically and 2026 third-party sources conflicted. Our policy is ranges or links — never invented numbers.

Pricing & plans — verified

Verified on the official pricing page on 2026-09-06 where possible. Dollar figures for paid tiers are omitted deliberately: the page prices dynamically and independent 2026 sources disagreed. The plan structure and feature lists below are verified; the numbers live at the linked official checkout.

Proton Free$0 — verified · —ForeverUnlimited logins/devices, 10 aliases, passkeys

Pass FamilySee official checkout · —Monthly/annualPass Plus for 6 users, family admin panel
Proton UnlimitedSee official checkout · —Monthly/annualPass + Mail + Calendar + VPN + Drive bundle

A 30-day money-back guarantee applies to paid plans per the official page. If a third party quotes you a Pass Plus figure without a check date, treat it skeptically — we found $1.99–2.99/mo in 2026 sources for the same tier, which is exactly why we don't pick one.

Feature-by-feature analysis

Free tier

The most capable free tier after Bitwarden's — and the only one that includes email aliases (10). Unlimited devices free is something NordPass explicitly does not offer.

Hide-my-email aliases

Alias generation is Pass's signature convenience: unique addresses per site that forward to your inbox, making tracking and breaches easier to contain. Unlimited on paid tiers; 10 free.

Integrated 2FA authenticator

Pass Plus stores and generates TOTP codes — same pattern as Bitwarden Premium's authenticator, reducing app sprawl.

Swiss privacy framework

Proton AG operates under Swiss jurisdiction with a privacy-first track record (Proton Mail). For users whose threat model includes jurisdiction, this is a primary differentiator.

Open source

Pass clients are open source like Bitwarden's — verifiable rather than trust-on-faith.

Maturity

The honest limitation: Pass launched more recently than every competitor here. Independent 2026 coverage praises its pace of development; the app experience still trails 1Password today. If you adopt, expect fast iteration rather than perfection.

Ease of use

Evidence-based: clean, understandable apps and a straightforward import flow; autofill works across the standard browsers/extensions. It is slightly less slick than 1Password and slightly less battle-tested — consistent with independent 2026 assessments — but nothing that would block a typical household.

Security

End-to-end, zero-knowledge encryption on Proton's infrastructure; open-source clients; Swiss jurisdiction; optional high-security program (Proton Sentinel) on paid tiers (vendor-documented). No known vault breaches as of 2026-09-06. Note: Proton services have complied with lawful requests in criminal cases historically (documented publicly for Proton Mail) — jurisdiction protects against sweeping data collection, not against valid legal process.

Pros & cons

Pros
  • Truly usable free tier: unlimited logins and devices, plus 10 aliases (verified)
  • Open source with Swiss jurisdiction — the strongest privacy posture in our set
  • Integrated 2FA authenticator and unlimited aliases on Plus
  • 30-day money-back guarantee (verified) de-risks trying paid tiers
  • Bundle value with Proton Mail/VPN/Drive on Unlimited
Cons
  • Youngest product in the set — less polish and fewer years of operational hardening
  • Paid-tier prices not verifiable as stable figures on launch day (dynamic pricing)
  • Family/admin features less mature than 1Password's
  • Aliases require trusting Proton with metadata of your alias traffic (inherent to the design)

Alternatives to consider first

  • 1Password — Pick for the most polished apps and family controls if jurisdiction is not a factor

    Is Proton Pass really free and unlimited?
    The free tier is verified as unlimited for logins, notes, and credit cards across unlimited devices, including passkey support and 10 email aliases (official pricing page, checked 2026-09-06). Paid tiers add sharing, unlimited aliases, 2FA authenticator, dark-web monitoring, and attachments.

    We don't quote a number because the official page prices dynamically and 2026 sources disagreed ($1.99–2.99/mo range). The honest path: check the official pricing page — and remember the 30-day money-back guarantee effectively makes trying it free.
    Is Proton Pass open source?
    Yes — the apps are open source, consistent with Proton's practice across Mail, Drive, and VPN. Combined with Swiss jurisdiction, this is the core of its privacy pitch.
    Proton Pass vs Bitwarden — which free tier wins?
    Bitwarden for maturity and ecosystem breadth; Proton Pass if aliases and jurisdiction matter to you. Both are unlimited for logins/devices. Our full decision framework is in the pillar guide.
    The bottom line

    The privacy pick that's free where it counts — adopt for the principles, with eyes open about maturity.

Quick verdict

Buy 1Password if a refined, effortless experience for you or your family justifies paying roughly $28–47 more per year than Bitwarden Premium. Buy Bitwarden if you lead with value, want a genuinely unlimited free tier, or require open source and self-hosting. Both use zero-knowledge encryption and are safe, reputable choices — this is a values decision, not a safety decision.

Best for 1Password

Households and professionals who want the most polished apps, best family sharing UX, and features like Travel Mode — and consider experience worth $3.99/mo (verified regular price; $2.99 first-year promo).

Best for Bitwarden

Budget-conscious users (including 'free'), open-source advocates, self-hosters, and families who want 6 premium accounts for $3.99/mo total ($0.67/person at capacity).

Choose 1Password if…

  • You'll pay for polish: 1Password's apps, autofill, and organization are the category benchmark
  • Family sharing is central — unlimited shared vaults with the smoothest admin and recovery UX
  • You want Watchtower's proactive security guidance and Travel Mode
  • You're a new customer — the verified first-year promo ($2.99 Individual / $4.49 Families) softens year one
  • You prefer not to think about billing terms: one annual plan, transparent regular pricing

Choose Bitwarden if…

  • Price is the constraint: free forever, or $19.80/yr for Premium (both verified)
  • You want open-source code, self-hosting, or a US/EU-hosted, audit-friendly stack
  • Your household is up to 6 people — Families covers 6 premium accounts at $3.99/mo total
  • You want an integrated TOTP authenticator without paying 1Password prices
  • You're advising a mixed group: Bitwarden's free tier means nobody is priced out of basic security

The key difference

You are choosing between experience and leverage. 1Password sells the best-finished product in the category at $47.88/yr (Individual, regular). Bitwarden gives the security fundamentals away free and sells convenience for $19.80/yr. Neither has a meaningful security-quality advantage for typical users; the difference is app polish, family UX, business tooling — and price.

If both fit your budget and needs, let two questions decide. (1) Who is this for? Families who want zero friction → 1Password; mixed groups or budget-shared households → Bitwarden.     Can I switch from one to the other easily?
    Yes — both support standard CSV export/import, and Bitwarden documents direct imports from 1Password. Budget an hour, change your master password everywhere after moving, and keep the old export encrypted while you verify.

Contenders that didn't make the list

  • LastPass — Its breach history (documented incidents in 2014, 2015, and major 2022 disclosures) keeps it off our recommendation list for new users despite competitive pricing (~$3/mo reported). Switchers: our alternatives coverage addresses migration.

Reputable ones are: zero-knowledge encryption means the vendor cannot read your vault. The realistic risks are a weak master password and phishing — mitigations (strong generator, breach alerts, passkeys) are built into every manager we recommend.

item.title: Free vs Paid Password Managers (2026): What Free Really Gets You
item.dc:creator: readmehub
item.content:encoded:
The direct answer

Free is genuinely enough for many people in 2026 — but only the right free. Bitwarden Free (unlimited passwords/devices, verified) and Proton Pass Free (unlimited logins/devices plus 10 aliases, verified) are complete products; NordPass Free (one device) and most 'free trials' are marketing. Pay only when you hit four specific moments: you want an integrated 2FA authenticator, you need emergency access, you want breach coaching beyond alerts, or you want the polish tier of the category (1Password, paid-only).

The free tiers, verified (2026-09-06)

Not all free tiers are the same product category. Verified on official pages:

Swipe to see all columns →
['Manager', 'Free limits', 'The catch', 'Verdict']
ManagerFree limitsThe catchVerdict
Bitwarden FreeUnlimited passwords, unlimited devicesNo integrated TOTP authenticator, no emergency access, no vault health reportsThe real thing — our default free recommendation
Proton Pass FreeUnlimited logins/notes/cards, unlimited devices, 10 email aliases, passkeysNo item sharing beyond basics, no dark-web monitoring, aliases capped at 10The real thing, plus aliases — younger product
NordPass FreeUnlimited passwords, one device at a timeOne device is disqualifying for most multi-device humansA demo, not a tier
1PasswordNo free tier14-day trial insteadPaid-only by design

The four moments when paying pays off

  • You want your 2FA codes inside your vault Bitwarden Premium ($19.80/yr verified) and Proton Pass Plus integrate TOTP generation — one less app, autofilled codes. Security practitioners debate vaulting 2FA (single point of failure); for most people the usability gain wins.
  • Someone needs access if you can't act Emergency access (Bitwarden Premium, Proton Pass Plus) or 1Password Families recovery. If your family would be locked out of your accounts, this is the feature you're actually buying.
  • You keep reusing passwords despite alerts Free tiers alert; paid tiers coach — vault health reports, weak/reused dashboards, breach monitoring (Bitwarden Premium, Proton Pass Plus, NordPass paid). The upgrade is behavioral, not cryptographic.
  • Daily friction is costing you If autofill friction makes you fall back to browser storage or reused passwords, the $3.99/mo polish of 1Password is the correct purchase. The best manager is the one you actually use.

What we'd do

Start free with Bitwarden (or Proton Pass if aliases/jurisdiction appeal). Re-evaluate in 90 days: if you're hitting the four moments, Bitwarden Premium at $19.80/yr is the cheapest complete upgrade we verified; 1Password is the comfort upgrade. Skip 'lifetime' impulses without reading terms — and note that paying never changes the encryption; it buys convenience, recovery, and coaching.

FAQ

Is a free password manager safe?
Bitwarden's and Proton's free tiers use the same zero-knowledge encryption as their paid tiers — payment buys features, not stronger cryptography. Verified on official documentation, 2026-09-06.
Why is NordPass's free tier limited?
It allows one active device at a time — by design, to drive upgrades. Unlimited-password-but-one-device is effectively a trial for anyone with a phone and a computer.

item.title: Password Manager vs Browser Autofill (2026): The Honest Comparison
item.dc:creator: readmehub
item.content:encoded:
The direct answer

Browser autofill is fine for low-stakes browsing and better than reusing passwords. A dedicated manager wins on everything that matters at scale: cross-browser and app coverage, breach and reuse detection, secure sharing, passkey portability, and survival of browser reinstalls. The honest framing: autofill is a convenient floor, not a strategy — and the migration from one to the other is about an hour.

Where browser autofill genuinely suffices

If you browse in one browser on one device, use unique passwords, and don't care about breach monitoring, Google/Apple/Safari password features have improved enough (passkey support, breach alerts in some ecosystems) that the gap is narrower than security Twitter claims. Apple's ecosystem (iCloud Keychain) in particular is a competent closed-garden solution.

Where the floor gives way

Swipe to see all columns →
['Need', 'Browser autofill', 'Dedicated manager']
NeedBrowser autofillDedicated manager
All browsers + native appsOne browser only; apps inconsistentEvery browser, plus iOS/Android apps
Breach & reuse detectionPartial, ecosystem-dependentCore feature (Watchtower, Vault Health, breach scanners)
Secure sharing (family/team)NoneVault/item sharing, emergency access
Passkeys across ecosystemsImproving, but locked to vendorPortable across platforms (verified: Bitwarden, Proton Pass, 1Password)
Survives switching browsers/devicesExport/import painVault is the product
Encrypted storage of more than passwordsLimitedCards, identities, notes, attachments, 2FA codes

The one-hour migration

  • Pick your manager (Bitwarden free is the default answer — see the free-vs-paid guide).
  • Export passwords from your browser (documented per-browser: Chrome/Safari/Edge settings → passwords → export CSV).
  • Import via the manager's documented importer; delete the CSV immediately.
  • Install the browser extension + mobile app, disable browser save-password prompts, change your master password habit for two weeks.
  • Turn on 2FA for the vault itself. Done — and the vault's breach/reuse report will probably surprise you.

FAQ

Is browser password storage encrypted?
Yes — modern browsers encrypt saved passwords, typically keyed to your OS account. The difference vs dedicated managers is portability, cross-app coverage, and monitoring, not raw encryption.
Can I use both?
Many people run both during migration. Long-term, running both invites divergence: pick one source of truth for anything you care about.

Bitwarden is our value and transparency benchmark — so alternatives matter only for specific reasons: polish (choose 1Password), lowest long-term price for one user (choose NordPass on a 2-year term), privacy jurisdiction plus aliases (choose Proton Pass), or total offline control (choose KeePassXC). What Bitwarden does well (why people choose it)

  • Cheapest complete premium: $19.80/yr (verified)

Where it may not fit — the actual reasons people switch

App polish

The apps are functional but utilitarian; users coming from Apple-ecosystem polish or 1Password trials notice immediately.

Evidence: Consistently noted across independent 2026 reviews; UX is Bitwarden's most-cited trade-off.

Guided simplicity

Organizations/collections sharing concepts add a learning curve that simpler products avoid by offering less.

Evidence: Documented in Bitwarden's own help structure (organizations vs folders vs collections).

Premium price momentum

Premium rose from $10 to $19.80/yr in January 2026 (reported by multiple sources). Still cheap; the direction is worth noting for renewal planning.

The best alternative, by reason

"I want a more polished experience" → 1Password

Verified price: $3.99/mo (verified; $2.99 first year). The category's experience benchmark: better autofill, organization, Watchtower guidance, and family recovery. You pay ≈2× Bitwarden Premium for it.

"I want the cheapest paid tier, single user" → NordPass Premium (2-year term)

Verified price: ≈$1.3–2/mo range (verified range). Undercuts Bitwarden Premium on long terms with a slicker app — trade-offs: closed source, one-device free tier, and multi-year commitment.

"I want stronger privacy jurisdiction + aliases" → Proton Pass

Verified price: Free tier strong; Plus at official checkout. Swiss jurisdiction, open source, 10 free aliases (verified). Younger product; share its open-source ethos with Bitwarden but not its maturity.

Match your actual complaint to a product that fixes it — not to a longer feature list. item.dc:creator: readmehub

The honest preamble

Most 'methodology' pages describe a laboratory. Here is ours: we have not conducted hands-on laboratory testing. ReadMeHub reviews are research-based — built from verified vendor documentation, official pricing pages, published security audits, and consistent independent evidence, each fact dated. Where we characterize user experience, we say so as evidence-based assessment, not personal testing. We think a methodology you can actually audit beats a fictional one.

Evaluation criteria

Six criteria, in priority order:

  • 1. Security architecture — encryption approach, zero-knowledge design, audit history (as documented by vendors and auditors).
  • 2. Price & value — verified pricing across billing terms, per-person math for plans, free-tier honesty. Prices must be verified at official sources to appear in tables.
  • 3. Trust & transparency — open source status, jurisdiction, breach history, corporate transparency.
  • 4. Ease of use — onboarding friction and cross-platform consistency, assessed from documented evidence and labeled as such.
  • 5. Feature completeness — the features that carry real decisions: passkeys, 2FA integration, sharing, recovery, breach monitoring.
  • 6. Recovery & sharing — emergency access, family controls, inheritance: where real life actually tests a product.

Evidence rules

  • Prices: verified at the official checkout/pricing page, with a 'Last verified' date on the page. If a figure can't be verified (dynamic pricing), we publish a labeled range or omit the number and link the source.
  • Claims: vendor documentation or ≥2 independent corroborating sources; vendor-only claims are framed as vendor-reported.
  • Ratings: none, until a genuine scoring methodology with real evaluation exists. Qualitative verdicts only.
  • Testing: never implied. If we test hands-on in the future, pages will say exactly what was tested, when, and by whom.
  • Deals: VERIFIED, OFFICIAL, UNVERIFIED, or NONE — with check dates; unverified offers never display amounts.

Update policy

Money pages carry a verification date and are re-checked on a ≤45-day cycle (30 days for deals). Material changes are noted on the page. If a page has gone stale past its cycle, our QA flags it internally — and you can flag it too.

What we refuse to do

Fabricate ratings, reviews, or testing. Invent coupon codes. Manufacture urgency. Let commissions order a ranking. Publish prices we can't verify. Create doorway pages. These rules cost us short-term revenue; they are the product.
